title: A/B Testing LLM Features — GrowthBook, Statsig, and the Vibes Problem

questions.question: What is the precise distinction between evals and A/B tests in the lesson?
options: Only A/B tests are required; the lesson treats offline evals as optional once online testing exists
Evals answer "can the model do the job?" on a labeled set; A/B tests answer "do users care?" with live randomized traffic
Evals are user-facing; A/B tests are offline — exactly backwards from how the lesson draws the line
They are interchangeable, since the lesson treats a passing eval as sufficient evidence users prefer a change
questions.explanation: The lesson draws the line precisely: evals are offline against a labeled set and answer whether the model can do the task; A/B tests are online with randomized live traffic and answer whether users actually care about the change.

questions.question: What does CUPED do for an experiment?
options: Disables multiple-comparison correction, trading Bonferroni or Benjamini-Hochberg for a raw p-value
Replaces sequential testing entirely, so mSPRT and confidence-sequence peeking are no longer needed
Increases sample size by hiring more users, the manual alternative to CUPED's statistical adjustment
Regresses out pre-period variance before comparing post-period, typically reducing variance 30-70% and boosting effective sample size
questions.explanation: The lesson describes CUPED (Controlled-experiments Using Pre-Experiment Data) as regressing out pre-period variance before comparing the post-period, typically cutting variance 30-70% and raising effective sample size for free.

questions.question: Why do you need multiple-comparison corrections (Bonferroni or Benjamini-Hochberg) when running many A/Bs?
options: Running 20 tests at 95% confidence produces one false positive by chance; corrections control family-wise error or false discovery rate
They are required by GDPR, which the lesson cites as the legal basis for Bonferroni and Benjamini-Hochberg
They are only needed for sequential tests, not for the fixed-sample-size A/B tests the lesson otherwise describes
They speed up experiments by letting you stop earlier than a properly powered fixed-sample test would allow
questions.explanation: The lesson notes that running 20 A/B tests at 95% confidence produces roughly one false positive by chance alone, and Bonferroni (tightening per-test alpha) or Benjamini-Hochberg (controlling false-discovery rate) correct for that.

questions.question: What does SRM (sample ratio mismatch) detect?
options: Slow tokenizer performance, a latency issue the lesson does not connect to randomization checks
Memory leaks in the experiment platform, an infrastructure issue rather than a randomization check
An assignment-hash bug producing a delivered split that diverges from the intended (e.g. 47/53 when targeting 50/50)
PII leakage, a data-handling issue the lesson does not connect to sample ratio mismatch detection
questions.explanation: The lesson describes SRM checks as flagging when the assignment hash delivers a split that diverges from the intended one (e.g. 47/53 instead of the targeted 50/50), signaling a broken randomization.

questions.question: Why does LLM non-determinism require buffering sample size?
options: It is irrelevant to power calculations, since the lesson treats LLM outputs as effectively IID
Non-determinism reduces required samples, since varying outputs average out variance faster
It only matters offline, since the lesson ties non-determinism strictly to eval-set scoring, not live A/B power
It violates IID assumptions; effective sample size drops, so multiply required size by roughly 1.3-1.5x as a safety margin
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that traditional power calculations assume IID observations, but LLM non-determinism means effective sample size is lower than nominal, so the required sample size should be multiplied by roughly 1.3-1.5x as a safety margin.

questions.question: How does the lesson contrast Statsig and GrowthBook?
options: Statsig is all-in-one SaaS (acquired by OpenAI Sept 2025, $1.1B); GrowthBook is open-source MIT, warehouse-native, with Bayesian/Frequentist/Sequential engines and CUPED/SRM/BH
Identical feature sets, since the lesson treats Statsig and GrowthBook as interchangeable on every axis
Statsig is warehouse-native only, reading directly from Snowflake or BigQuery with no hosted option
GrowthBook is closed source, sold only as a managed SaaS product with no self-host option
questions.explanation: The lesson contrasts Statsig -- hosted, all-in-one SaaS, acquired by OpenAI for $1.1B in September 2025 -- with GrowthBook, which is open-source MIT, warehouse-native, and ships Bayesian/Frequentist/Sequential engines plus CUPED, SRM checks, and Bonferroni/Benjamini-Hochberg corrections.
